mysterious and the uncanny, who is not secure of himself,
who is aware that his life is both driven onward and
thwarted by forces which are more powerful than himself,
lives in anxiety; and in his anxiety he worships these trans-
cendent forces as gods. And even when finally he concludes
that the various powers are one and the same, he is still not
freed from this anxiety; for he still does not know the one
God who is Lord of heaven and earth.
The more gods or the more altars there are, so many more
the symbols of human fear. The altar consecrated "to an
unknown god" was also such a symbol. For such altars (and
they bear too the inscription: "To the god whom it con-
cerns") arise from this enveloping fear: here is a god at
work whom I do not yet know and whose name I do not yet
know! Hence he must have an altar at which he may be so
to speak anonymously worshipped.
2. The second factor emerges from the words of Paul:
"The God who made the world and everything in it...
does not live in shrines made by man" (v. 24ff.), "and we
ought not to think that the Deity is like gold or silver or
stone, a representation by the art and imagination of man"
(v. 29). Here again the superstitious element does not reside
in false conceptions. For by the time of Paul those old
conceptions had been superseded, according to which God
had a human form, was bound to a particular place, and
needed to be sustained by a human worship and culture.
The real superstitious element resides rather in the inten-
tion which lies at the basis of the sensuous representation and
cultic worship of the Deity. That intention is to secure control
of the divine. Religion is the attempt to conquer the fear of
those dark powers which, springing from nature and fate and
the depths of the human soul, stand threateningly across
man's path; it is the attempt to exorcize these powers by
